title: Protect the Children
subtitle: A lot of people say it. Here’s what I mean by it.
body:
“Protect the children” is my creed. My motto. My battle cry. If you’ve seen me on LinkedIn or Facebook, there’s a good chance you’ve seen a post of mine end with it.

I wrote it to a mother who lost her son, in a letter that asked her for nothing. It sits under almost everything I build.

Two weeks ago I watched the biggest companies on earth say it too. They said it while they sued to stop a law written to do it.

So before anybody else defines my creed for me, I’m going to.

Here is one week in November.

On Tuesday, Google announced that its AI tools, and Google Search itself, would be switched off on the school accounts it gives to kids until an administrator turns them on. Good. Then Google’s vice president for education told the New York Times there was a catch: Search and AI are “deeply integrated,” so a school that kept the AI off would lose Search too. By that afternoon, after the pushback, Google said they were separate switches after all. Search still comes with AI built into it.

On Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok each sued California to block a law that keeps personalized feeds and autoplay away from kids under sixteen. Google’s spokesman said, “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built.” Meta said the law would force it to strip out features that keep teens’ experience age-appropriate, or cut thousands of California teens off.

Three months earlier, Meta agreed to pay up to eighteen billion dollars and add stronger child-safety measures, settling claims brought by nearly every state in the country.

Settle in August. Sue in November. Both in the name of the kids.

The same week, a family in North Carolina sued Google over their thirteen-year-old daughter. The complaint says she never went looking for Gemini. It showed up in an ordinary search on her school Chromebook, and over months it became the place she took her darkest thoughts. It says the chatbot helped her plan for her own death and coached her to hide what she was feeling from her family. What finally caught it, the complaint says, wasn’t Google. It was the school’s monitoring software, months in. These are allegations, no court has ruled, and Google says it is reviewing the claims, takes them very seriously, and that its systems aim to prevent harmful conversations.

That same week, the BBC tested an AI stuffed bunny sold for children as young as three. A reporter asked it what “sexual” meant. It answered with a crisis script meant for someone talking about self-harm, including the line “I can’t help with killing you.” The BBC couldn’t find out who makes it.

Every one of them was protecting the children. The company that settled. The companies that sued. The state that passed the law. The bunny with no maker.

I can think of only one phrase in this country that gets said more and means less: thoughts and prayers, and it’s usually after a kid has died.

I have a personal reason not to trust it, including when I say it.

When I was a teenager I was sent to a residential school for troubled kids. That’s how programs like it were sold to families: as protection. Some of the people there saved my life. Years later I went back and worked there. What happened in between belongs in a book, not here.

What I can give you here is the public record. In 2007, government auditors told Congress they had found thousands of allegations of abuse at residential programs for troubled teens, some involving deaths, and that no agency anywhere kept a full national count. In 2024, a two-year Senate investigation of four of the biggest operators concluded the abuse wasn’t a few bad apples. It was built into a business model paid for with public money meant for kids. The operators dispute it.

That’s what the phrase can buy when nobody checks. A locked door. A business plan.

It still happens in quieter ways. The Electronic Frontier Foundation opposed California’s new law too, for its own reasons: it argues the law will push platforms into age checks on every user, adults included. That isn’t a tech company talking point. It’s a real cost. Protecting kids can turn into watching everyone, and the people who do the watching rarely give the cameras back.

The phrase is a key. It opens doors. That’s exactly why so many people who want doors opened keep picking it up.

So here is what I mean when I say it. Four lines. Hold me to them.

Test it before it touches them.

I love this technology and I want it integrated into everything, including the toys and tools my children will use, which is why I am so desperate to make sure that it is tested. A thirteen-year-old shouldn’t be the test. Neither should a three-year-old holding a bunny. The test comes first. It’s written down before it runs, done by someone who isn’t paid for the answer, and published even when it embarrasses the person who ran it. That’s what I’m building E.D.A.I. to do. At its true size today, it’s a prototype with one test plan sealed on a public ledger. I say that every time.

This one is mine. My son is seven, and he’s working out friendship the hard way. Not long ago, in the car, I opened a voice conversation with my AI so we could trade jokes and riddles. When we got out, he told me it was his best friend. I told him it isn’t a real person, and that we’d talk more about it. Back in the car he asked to talk to it again, and the first thing he said when it came on was, “You’re my best friend.” I stopped him. We don’t start saying that, to ourselves or to the machine.

Put a name on the desk.

Every product that reaches a kid crossed somebody’s desk, and somebody said yes. When it goes wrong, I want that name to be findable, not just the logo. Last month I went looking for one person who built, ran or profited from a chatbot named in a child’s death and has faced a consequence you can point to. I couldn’t find one. I’m still looking.

One of the chatbot companies named in those lawsuits, Character.AI, is in bankruptcy court right now, selling what it built. The first bidder named on the record was Disney, for twenty million dollars, and its deal is a license to some of the company’s technology, not the users’ chats. The bid for everything else, the app, the models, the user accounts and the chats themselves, is ten million dollars, from a company called Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC. Reporters checking Delaware’s records found it was formed the day before it was named. The filing doesn’t say who owns it.

I’m not accusing anyone. I’m asking: who is it, and what do they want with all those conversations, some of them children’s? If you have more access than I do, find out. We should be able to know. Ten million dollars for everything those kids told a machine. Follow the money. That’s the piece I promised you last time, and it’s next.

Don’t make them the watched.

No dossier on a kid. No label stuck on a kid from the outside. No watching every child in the name of keeping them safe. That cuts both ways in the North Carolina story. The software that caught what the chatbot missed may have saved that girl. It’s the same kind of software that reads a lot of kids’ schoolwork every day. Both are true. So I want to know who reads those flags, and what happens to the kids they get wrong.

See them.

Before the tests, the laws and the lawsuits, there is a kid alone in a room who needs one adult to notice. I worked a suicide prevention line. I founded a nonprofit for teenagers a lot of people had written off, and my students made a film about cyberbullying that won an award at the All American High School Film Festival. I was one of those kids myself. Every time I saw a kid saved, it wasn’t a filter that did it. It was a person who noticed. Sometimes the last person you’d expect. Someone I couldn’t stand saved my life when I was a teenager. I’ll tell you that story when it’s ready.

In Apocaloptimist I ended on upgrading yourself, then making them show their work. Here’s what that looks like at my house.

My kids carry school Chromebooks. I don’t know yet everything that’s switched on inside them. So I’m asking, as a parent, and the people at our district have been generous with their time. Friendly questions, not accusations. You can ask the same three at your kids’ school.

Which AI tools are on for students, and who decided?

What happens to what my kid types into them?

Can families read the rules?

And the upgrade part is mine before it’s anybody else’s: my phone at the dinner table, my attention, whether my kids find me there when they look up.

The people leading this fight now are mostly parents who lost a child to it. Their children’s names aren’t mine to use. But if you care, you can find them online. They aren’t hidden, and they shouldn’t be. We should remember them, and honor them by fighting this together.

Some of the people in this fight I’ve come to know. They put their lives behind it, not just their words, and I want you to know they exist.

Kristin Bride runs The Carson J. Bride Effect. It carries her son’s name because she chose to carry it. After he died, she sued Snapchat and the anonymous messaging apps that ran inside it, and Snap pulled those apps from its platform. She carries this to lawmakers, too. In 2023 she testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee and asked Congress to pass the Kids Online Safety Act. This June she stood with senators to call the House’s weaker version, the KIDS Act, “a slap in the face to all the parents.”

Heat Initiative, led by its CEO, Brooke Istook, holds tech companies accountable for what their products do to kids. This month, with ParentsTogether Action, it wrote to the judge in the Character.AI bankruptcy, asking that safety conditions travel with whatever gets sold and that no chat data move through the technology license.

Nicki Petrossi hosts Scrolling 2 Death, a podcast for parents worried about social media, screen time and the devices schools hand our kids. If you’re a parent, start there.

Others I haven’t met yet, but I follow their work, and I want you to know it.

Common Sense Media tested AI toys this year and told parents plainly: no AI toy companion for a child five or under, and extreme caution for ages six to twelve. In May it launched a Youth AI Safety Institute to test the AI products kids use most and publish what it finds. Some of its funders make AI products it tests, Anthropic and the OpenAI Foundation among them, and it says so openly.

Dr. Ying Xu, an assistant professor at Harvard’s Graduate School of Education, is running the first study of its kind. Her team built its own AI toy and has begun testing it with young children, comparing their play with it against play with ordinary toys. The aim is the first hard evidence for what age these toys are right for.

Fairplay fights to keep marketing away from children. Last November it put out a warning to parents against AI toys, signed by more than 150 groups and experts.

ParentsSOS is twenty families bound together by the loss of a child. They are working to get the Kids Online Safety Act passed.

Public Citizen, a consumer watchdog since 1971, put out a warning in September with Heat Initiative and Mothers Against Media Addiction: AI is not a toy. It is calling on states to ban AI chatbot toys, and it keeps a running tracker of every state’s bills to protect kids from manipulative chatbots.

When Disney stepped forward in the Character.AI bankruptcy, Ilana Beller of Public Citizen called it “a sad and scary example of a corporation choosing profit over the wellbeing of our children.” I don’t necessarily believe that is the full story. But it’s a question worth exploring.

And one company. mpathic is a clinician-founded AI safety company. It builds tests for how AI models handle high-risk conversations, among them suicide and eating disorders, and it does this work, in its own words, “especially in high-risk moments involving youth, mental health, and medical care.” Full disclosure: I’ve applied to work there. I’m naming them anyway, because I’m trying to be as helpful and as engaged in this as I can.

Follow them. If you’re moved to, support them. They were in this fight long before I was.

But outside of all that, there’s something very real and hyper-local that you can do.

Watch The AI Doc: Or How I Became an Apocaloptimist. It follows a filmmaker getting ready to become a father, trying to understand the world his child will inherit. The question under the whole film is the one every parent I know is carrying: will my children have a future? You can watch it at home now.

Then don’t watch it alone. I’m starting a group of parents near me to break it down together. We haven’t met yet, so none of what follows has happened. It’s the plan. We want each of us to walk out with one action from this list:

  1. One short letter each to our representatives, from a shared draft the group agrees on.

  2. A newsletter with one action per issue.

  3. Opening doors for anyone in the room with a government contact.

  4. Weighing whether a petition is worth the effort before anyone starts one.

  5. Each of us bringing one more parent.

What the letter asks for is still open. The candidate on the table comes from Apocaloptimist: independent testing that the labs pay for but don’t get to choose.

You can do this in your town. Watch it. Gather a few parents. Learn it together first, so you can teach it to your kids. Then write your representatives together. The way I took the film’s ending, the work happens in the rooms we’re already in.

If you want company doing it, Humans in Control is a nonprofit I’ve connected with. It calls itself a cross-partisan grassroots movement for commonsense rules on AI, and protecting kids is in its mission. Its plan is the same one: educate the people around you, bring in the ones you already talk to, and make sure the people who represent you hear from you. This month its supporters held AI Reality Check conversations with their neighbors in more than thirty states.

I don’t know how to keep every kid safe. Nobody does, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Maybe a bunny.

What I know is that the phrase belongs to the kids. Not to whoever says it loudest in a court filing, and not to me either. I just get to promise what I mean by it.

Test it first. Put a name on the desk. Don’t make them the watched. See them.

Protect the children. Hold me to it.

If you or someone you love is struggling, call or text 988 in the US to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
